item.title: Are These Unsightly Bumps as Awful as They Look?
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Warts, or papillomas, typically affect young, immunosuppressed and older dogs
  • Since these growths are benign, they should really only be removed if they’re impinging on a dog’s quality of life
  • It can be helpful to view harmless papillomas on dogs as a window into their immunologic health
  • Since papillomatosis can be a sign that a dog has been over-vaccinated, it’s another reason to have your pet titer tested in lieu of automatic revaccination
  • In rare cases, a wart that keeps growing or changing may signal squamous cell carcinoma and should be evaluated promptly

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published June 9, 2019.

The medical term for warts is papillomas, because papilloma viruses — a group of DNA viruses — are responsible for the cauliflower-looking skin and mouth lesions that occur in dogs. The viruses typically affect three types of dogs:

  1. Young dogs, who tend to develop outbreaks of oral papillomatosis
  2. Immunosuppressed dogs, especially dogs who've received corticosteroids, for example, prednisone, or any drug that suppresses the immune system
  3. Older dogs, who often develop warts as they age

In veterinary medicine, it's assumed all dogs are exposed to papilloma viruses, but these opportunistic viruses tend to cause warts only in dogs with immune systems that aren't 100% healthy or dogs who are stressed. The good news is canine warts don't affect other species, so there's no need to worry that other members of your family, including kitties, will pick up the virus.

Dogs at Highest Risk for Papillomatosis

Young dogs usually develop oral papillomatosis (oral warts) that on very rare occasions can also cause warts to grow in the mucous membranes of the eye. These wart clusters often have a fleshy, cauliflower-like appearance.

The virus is most commonly spread by direct contact between dogs, such as when they lick or mouth each other, or share a toy. Oral papillomatosis typically occurs in dogs under 2 years of age whose immune systems are still immature, meaning their bodies aren't yet capable of mounting an effective immune response to eliminate the virus. Dogs who are immunoglobulin A (IgA)-deficient are also at risk.

Oral warts often spontaneously regress after a few months when the dog's immune system matures, recognizes the virus and resolves the outbreak.

However, in severe cases of oral warts in dogs with congenital immunodeficiency or IgA-deficiency, the body may not even recognize an immune response is required, so the virus rages on unchecked and the lesions in the mouth don't heal. These poor puppies can have literally hundreds of warts in their mouths, making it nearly impossible to eat or drink without excruciating pain.

Puppies and adult dogs who acquire severe oral papillomatosis should have their immunoglobulin levels checked immediately and begin oral immunotherapy and specific nutritional therapy to assist their bodies in fighting off not only the papilloma virus, but other potential pathogens.

Dogs with oral papillomatosis should be separated from other dogs until all the lesions have cleared. Diagnostic testing isn't necessary in most cases because veterinarians can clearly recognize the classic appearance of the warts in the mouth.

When to Consider Wart Removal

Because these growths are benign (they look terrible, but they're not cancerous), the general guideline is to remove them only if they're causing quality of life issues for the dog. item.title: When the Baby Teeth May Be Overstaying Their Welcome
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Retained deciduous teeth, also called retained baby teeth, occur when a puppy's or kitten's baby tooth does not fall out after the permanent tooth begins erupting beside it
  • Most puppies begin losing baby teeth at around 12 weeks and finish teething by about 6 months, while kittens follow a similar timeline as their adult teeth gradually replace their first set
  • A double row of teeth, bad breath, and reluctance to chew are common signs, though pets often hide dental pain remarkably well
  • Retained teeth can trap food and bacteria, increasing the risk of bad breath, gum disease, discomfort, and bite problems that may affect normal tooth and jaw development over time
  • Veterinarians typically treat retained teeth with extraction under anesthesia, while pet parents can support healthy teething by offering appropriate chew toys, practicing good dental care, and monitoring for problems

If you have ever looked inside your puppy or kitten's mouth and thought they seemed to have two sets of teeth, you are probably right. Retained deciduous teeth occur when a baby tooth does not fall out after the permanent tooth has already started coming in.1 While it may seem like a minor issue at first, catching it early can help prevent crowding, gum disease, and bite problems that may become harder to correct as your pet gets older.

What You Should Know About Teething

Teething is a normal part of puppyhood and kittenhood. As young pets grow, their baby teeth gradually fall out and are replaced by a permanent adult set. While the process can be messy and sometimes uncomfortable, most puppies and kittens move through it without any major issues.

  • Deciduous teeth are your pet's first set of teeth — Also known as milk teeth or baby teeth, they begin erupting during the first few weeks of life and are eventually replaced by permanent adult teeth.2

    Additionally, puppies typically begin getting their baby teeth between 3 and 4 weeks of age and develop a total of 28 teeth, while kittens usually start teething between 2 and 4 weeks of age and have 26 baby teeth.3
  • Dogs and cats follow a similar teething timeline — The Pawlicy Advisor blog explains that puppies typically begin losing baby teeth at around 12 weeks and finish teething by about 6 months, while kittens start shedding baby teeth around 12 weeks and begin getting adult incisors between 3 1/2 and 4 months.4
  • Teeth that are likely to stay put — According to VCA Animal Hospitals, the upper canine teeth are retained most often, followed by the lower canines and incisors. Premolars are affected less frequently, while molars are never involved because dogs and cats do not have baby molars. Genetics appears to be the primary reason this happens.5
  • Which canine breeds are at risk? Retained baby teeth are seen more often in purebred dogs and brachycephalic breeds, which include flat-faced dogs such as Bulldogs, Pugs, Boston Terriers, and Boxers. Toy breeds such as Chihuahuas, Maltese, and Yorkies commonly have retained deciduous teeth. However, larger dogs and cats can develop the condition as well, although this is rare.
  • Common teething symptoms — Increased chewing, drooling, mild appetite changes, and finding baby teeth around the house are all normal parts of teething. However, bad breath, swollen gums, chewing on one side, dropping food, or a baby tooth that remains in place at around 6 months of age may indicate a problem. Because pets are often good at concealing dental pain, it is a good idea to have these signs evaluated by your veterinarian.

Why Retained Teeth Are a Problem

The WellPets blog says that a retained baby tooth may not look like a serious issue, especially if your pet is still eating, playing, and acting normally. However, once a permanent tooth erupts beside a baby tooth that has not fallen out, both teeth need to compete for the same space. This crowding can alter the way adult teeth erupt and create problems that become more difficult to correct as a puppy or kitten grows.6

One of the biggest concerns is malocclusion, a condition in which the teeth of the upper and lower jaws no longer align properly. Retained teeth can create abnormal tooth contact, or "interlocking," that interferes with normal jaw growth and development. In severe cases, this can affect the way a pet bites, chews, and uses its mouth.

Retained teeth also create tight spaces where food, plaque, and bacteria can accumulate. Over time, this buildup can lead to tartar, gingivitis, and periodontitis, a serious infection of the gums and supporting tissues. Misaligned teeth may also rub against nearby soft tissues, causing pain, inflammation, infection, abnormal tooth wear, and even tooth fractures.7

How Vets Treat Stubborn Milk Teeth

Once a retained baby tooth has been identified, veterinarians typically recommend removing it, especially if the permanent tooth has already erupted beside it. This situation violates the dental "Rule of Succession," which states that one tooth should replace another, not share the same space.

Treatment involves a complete oral exam and dental radiographs (X-rays) performed under anesthesia to evaluate the tooth and its root. The entire tooth needs to be removed to prevent pain and infection. When extraction is performed early, the permanent tooth has a much better chance of erupting into its normal position.8

What You Can Do to Make Teething Easier for Your Pet

While retained baby teeth cannot be prevented because genetics plays a major role, there are several ways to make the teething process more comfortable for your puppy or kitten. A little extra support during these months can help soothe sore gums, encourage healthy chewing habits, and promote better dental health overall.9

  • Offer age-appropriate toys — Dental chew toys can help relieve teething discomfort and support the transition from baby teeth to adult teeth. Puppies can usually handle durable nylon or hard-rubber toys, while kittens should stick to softer options to avoid damaging their teeth.
  • Start a dental care routine early — Introducing a pet-safe toothbrush and toothpaste while your pet is young can help keep their teeth clean and make future brushing sessions much easier.
  • Consult your veterinarian — Dental treats, prescription dental diets, dental powders, and water additives may help support oral health, but it is always best to ask your veterinarian which options are appropriate for your pet.

Sources and References

  • 1 Good Dog Veterinary Care, Retained Deciduous Teeth in Dogs
  • 2,5,7 VCA Animal Hospitals, April 24, 2024
  • 3 Veterinary Partner, June 2, 2025
  • 4,9 Pawlicy Advisor, June 5, 2026
  • 6,8 WellPets, Retained Deciduous Teeth (Baby Teeth) in Dogs & Cats

item.title: Millions Love This Semi-Domesticated Pet — Do You?
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Experts disagree on the topic of domesticated cats, specifically whether feline companions are truly tame, or only semi-tame
  • Despite thousands of years living with and around humans, cats continue to walk on the wild side, unlike dogs and other domesticated animals
  • Dogs are believed to have been domesticated between 18,000 and 30,000 years ago, while cats' domestication is estimated at just 4,000 to 9,000 years ago
  • A genome study of a domestic cat named Cinnamon found only modest genetic changes linked to domestication, especially compared to dogs
  • Cats have retained their hunting instincts and could likely survive in the wild, while most modern dog breeds would not

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published September 26, 2015.

Apparently there's a raging controversy among various scientists and biologists about whether domesticated cats are actually domestic. The confusion is understandable, especially for anyone who shares their life with a kitty. There's a certain wild vibe about feline companions — even tiny kittens — no matter how long they've shared a home or snuggled on a lap.

Cats are the most popular pet worldwide, and have lived with humans for 10,000 years or so. But despite their long and close association with us, cats turn feral without human contact, and it's often difficult to "tame" a feral kitten once it reaches a certain age.

Another sign of Fluffy's wild side: it's unlikely she'll starve to death if she escapes into the great outdoors, since her instinct to hunt never diminishes.

Cats Are Only 'Semi-Domesticated'

An analysis of the genome of an Abyssinian cat, a domestic female named Cinnamon whose lineage was traced back several generations, revealed certain genes responsible for domestication. However, the researchers concluded that cats are only "semi-domesticated," especially when compared to dogs. From the study abstract:

"Cats are considered only a semi-domesticated species, because many populations are not isolated from wildcats and humans do not control their food supply or breeding.

We therefore predicted a relatively modest effect of domestication on the cat genome based on recent divergence from and ongoing admixture with wildcats, a relatively short human cohabitation time compared with dogs, and the lack of clear morphological and behavioral differences from wildcats, with docility, gracility, and pigmentation being the exceptions."1

Not everyone is buying the semi-domesticated label. "There's no difference between a domesticated cat and a domesticated anything else," according to Greger Larson, an evolutionary biologist at the University of Oxford. "Good luck trying to get a goat or a sheep to spend the night in your house."2

Do Cats Tame Themselves?

According to Smithsonian.com:

"In its simplest form, to domesticate an animal means to tame it, through breeding and training, to need and accept the care of humans."3

Dogs are believed to have been domesticated anywhere from 18,000 to 30,000 years ago, when they separated from their wolf ancestors and began spending their days and nights around humans.

Cats, on the other hand, seem to have begun their journey to domestication around 4,000 years ago according to some experts, or 8,000 to 9,000 years ago according to others.

Wes Warren, an associate professor of genetics at the Genome Institute at Washington University in St. Louis and lead author of the Cinnamon genome study, believes that around 5,000 years ago a commensal relationship developed between cats and humans. Humans initially desired cats as pets because they kept rodents away from food sources.

However, Warren says what isn't known is whether the relatively minor taming of cats has been caused by humans, or whether cats have essentially tamed themselves.

Genetic Differences Between Cats and Tigers

Cinnamon's genome was compared to the genomes of a tiger, a cow, a dog, and a human. Earlier genetic studies have shown that Felis catus (the domestic cat) and Felis silvestris (a small wildcat native to Africa, Europe, and Asia) are not all that different.

But Warren discovered some differences between Cinnamon and the tiger, especially in terms of behavior. He found genes in Cinnamon that would make her more likely to approach humans and interact with them, and also to seek rewards. These same genetic sequences are also starting to be uncovered in rabbits, horses, and other domesticated animals.

According to Smithsonian.com, "This is not evolution, but the effects of human interventions."

Over the years, humans have bred dogs much more selectively than cats, with the goal of producing specific behaviors and temperaments, among other characteristics. Cats have been bred primarily for looks, for example, fur colors or patterns. Interestingly, a domestic cat's stripes are still no different than a wildcat's stripes. And Warren adds:

"Cats have retained their hunting skills and they're less dependent on humans for their source of food. With most of the modern breeds of dog, if you were to release them into the wild, most would not survive."

So Are Feline Companions Domesticated … or Not?

Apparently that depends on your definition of "domesticated." Some experts believe it's a simple matter of being tame enough to live with humans from one generation to the next, and cats certainly qualify.

But others believe there's more to it — that domestication involves "complex genetic and behavioral changes that transform a creature inside out."

Warren believes cats cannot be considered domesticated under the second definition. He points out that there are affectionate cats, but there are also plenty of wary and aggressive cats, and he believes the spectrum of feline behavior is wider than what's seen in dogs. Warren also points to the notorious feline independent streak:

"Cats only come to you for affection when they feel like it," he says. "They pretty much take care of themselves."

The question is, if cats really don't need us, have they actually been domesticated by us?

This isn't a question many pet parents are desperate to answer. The occasional flashes of wildness seen in cats — both feline patients and cats at home — are often part of what makes them so endearing.

What's not to love about sharing your life with a beautiful animal who is at times a cuddly companion, and other times, a creature of the wild?

Sources and References

  • 1 Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Vol. 111, No. 48, November 10, 2014
  • 2 Slate, July 5, 2015
  • 3 Smithsonian.com, April 30, 2015

item.title: Looking for a More Natural Way to Fight Fleas?
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • A single flea lays up to 50 eggs a day, and only about 5% of a home's flea population is adult — the rest hide in bedding, carpets, and floor cracks
  • Effective yard-level moves include regular mowing, pruning shrubs to let in sunlight, clearing leaf litter, using cedar mulch as a barrier, and planting flea-repellent species like lavender and lemongrass
  • Home defense relies on thorough vacuuming, steam cleaning, weekly hot-water bedding washes, DIY soapy-water flea traps, and food-grade diatomaceous earth applied along carpets and baseboards
  • On-pet options include dilute apple cider vinegar rinses, repellent electromagnetic flea and tick tags, lemon deterrent sprays, gentle bathing, and flea combing — plus properly diluted essential oils like lavender, cedarwood, lemongrass, and rosemary used with caution
  • Skip garlic, salt, alcohol, undiluted tea tree oil, and dish soap as standalone treatments — and consider a holistic vet who addresses diet, immune support, and overall toxin load

Your dog is scratching again — you spot the telltale dirt in their fur, then that unmistakable little dark shape moving across their belly. It is happening — fleas are back.

For a growing number of pet parents, the immediate reach for a strong chemical or prescription product no longer feels like the only option. Concerns about long-term chemical exposure, sensitivity in individual pets, medication side effects, and impact on the wider environment have all pushed people to ask a fairly reasonable question: is there a more natural way to deal with these annoying parasites?

The short answer is yes, though it takes a little more strategy. Natural flea control tends to be less about a single silver-bullet product and more about a coordinated, multi-front approach. Here is what integrative and holistic veterinarians tend to reach for — and what to skip.

Know What You Are Up Against

Fleas are relentless. A single female flea can lay up to 50 eggs a day, and a small handful in your home can turn into a thousand-flea problem in about three weeks. Their life cycle ranges anywhere from 14 days to 12 months (depending on temperature, humidity, and the presence of a host),1 and only about 5% of the fleas in an infested home are adults — the rest are eggs, larvae, and pupae hiding in bedding, carpets, and floor cracks.2

That biology is why any single approach usually fails. Killing adult fleas without addressing the eggs, larvae, and pupae in the environment just resets the timer. The dogs and cats we treat live in a home that is already hosting the next generation.

Natural approaches work best when they take that whole ecosystem into account — the yard, the home, and the pet. Skip any one of those, and you are playing whack-a-mole. Depending on your geographic location, fleas may be a year-round problem, meaning managing the yard, home, and deterrents on your pet are a daily activity necessary to stay on top of the life cycle.

Start with the Yard

Since fleas usually hitch a ride from outside, making your yard less flea-friendly is one of the highest-leverage moves you can make. The goal is to disrupt the conditions fleas rely on — shade, moisture, and undisturbed cover — so that fewer of them ever get close enough to jump on your pet in the first place.3,4

  • Mow the lawn regularly — but not too short, since ants and spiders (natural flea predators) prefer a bit of height. The grass does need to be short enough, though, that the ground underneath is dry. The goal is to not provide a humid environment for the fleas
  • Prune shrubs and remove dead limbs to let sunlight and air reach the ground; fleas are sensitive to direct sun and require at least 50% humidity to reproduce
  • Clear leaf litter, brush piles, and standing debris — they are prime flea nurseries
  • Create a barrier of cedar mulch around your house; fleas dislike cedar's aromatic compounds
  • Plant flea-repellent species that thrive in your climate — lavender, spearmint, and lemongrass are common choices
  • Consider natural yard sprays with essential-oil-based active ingredients, applied as directed. These do require frequent application, especially after rains

These small changes make it harder for fleas to complete their life cycle in your outdoor environment, which reduces how many make it onto your pet in the first place.

Tackle Your Indoor Environment

If you already have fleas indoors, addressing the environment is as important as treating your pet. Most of the flea population lives in your carpet, bedding, and furniture — not on your dog or cat.5,6

  • Vacuum thoroughly and often — Focus on carpets, baseboards, under furniture, cushions, and pet beds. Empty the vacuum canister or bag outside immediately to prevent re-infestation.
  • Steam cleaning is another powerful tool — Heat and moisture kill flea eggs and larvae, and steam-cleaning carpets and upholstery can dramatically reduce the population without adding a single chemical to your home.
  • Wash all pet bedding and any blankets your pet uses — Use hot water and do this weekly during active infestations or if you live in states with heavy year-round flea burdens (such as the Southeastern United States). This kills eggs and larvae on contact.
  • A DIY flea trap can help too — Fill a shallow pan with soapy water and place it under a lamp overnight in a suspected hot spot. Fleas are drawn to the heat and light and drown in the water. It is not a cure, but it can knock down the free-roaming adult population and helps you gauge how much of an infestation you are actually dealing with.

Food-Grade Diatomaceous Earth

Food-grade diatomaceous earth (DE) is one of the most widely recommended natural options for the home. It is a fine white powder made from fossilized algae, and its microscopic sharp edges physically damage the outer shell of fleas while absorbing the oils from their bodies, causing them to dehydrate.

Sprinkle a thin layer along baseboards, under furniture, around pet beds, and into carpets. Leave it undisturbed for 24 to 48 hours, then vacuum thoroughly. You can reapply for stubborn infestations.

Two important safety notes: Always use food-grade DE, not pool-grade (which is chemically treated) and apply it carefully while wearing a mask to prevent inhalation. The fine dust can irritate lungs if inhaled, so also avoid raising clouds during application, and keep pets away from freshly powdered areas until you have swept or vacuumed.

Some holistic veterinarians do recommend applying it directly to a pet's coat, but this comes with real drawbacks: it can dry out skin, and inhalation is a genuine risk. Check with your vet before applying it directly to your dog or cat.7

On Your Pet: Rinses, Sprays, and Baths

For the pet themselves, several natural options are gentle enough for regular use. These approaches work best as part of a consistent routine rather than a one-time treatment, since fleas can keep hitching a ride any time your pet steps outside. Please note, these treatments are geared at repelling adult fleas; most of these do not kill the adult fleas or address the other life stages.8,9

  • Apple cider vinegar rinse — A diluted apple cider vinegar spray (roughly a 50-50 mix with water) applied to your dog's coat — avoiding the eyes, ears, and any broken skin — can help make the environment less hospitable for fleas. Do a small patch test first to make sure your dog does not react. Apple cider vinegar, even diluted, can be drying to the skin and can cause GI upset if licked off the skin and fur. Also, the flea deterrent effect fades as the smell fades, so reapplication is necessary.
  • Lemon deterrent — Simmer four lemon slices with a tablespoon of salt in 6 cups of water for two minutes, then let it steep overnight. Apply to your dog's coat after bathing. Repels fleas thanks to naturally occurring limonene. Avoid the eyes and any raw skin. As with the vinegar, this can be drying to the skin and the repellent effect fades as the scent fades. Also, caution with using this around cats; limonene in high concentrations is toxic to cats.
  • A natural bath — A combination of gentle pet shampoo, warm water, and a dilute vinegar rinse can knock down live fleas and freshen the coat. Repeat weekly for dogs during flea season.
  • Frequent combing — A fine-toothed flea comb dipped between passes in a bowl of soapy water is one of the most direct — and least controversial — ways to physically remove fleas from your pet. Focus on the neck, base of the tail, belly, and hind legs.
  • Electromagnetic flea tags — Flea and tick repellent electromagnetic tags are available on the market. They have to stay on the pet (usually hanging from the collar) at all times for best effectiveness; while they do not repel all fleas, they can significantly decrease the flea load.

Essential Oils: Powerful but Not Casual

Essential oils are the most talked-about natural flea repellents. Several — including lavender, lemongrass, cedarwood, rosemary, and geranium — have well-documented insect-repellent properties and are used in many pet-safe natural flea products.10,11

But essential oils are also concentrated compounds with real biological activity, and misuse can cause harm. A few ground rules integrative veterinarians emphasize:

  • Always dilute before use — a few drops in a carrier oil like fractionated coconut, or in a large volume of water for spray applications. Talk to your veterinarian for more information on dilution ratios, and if using a commercial pet product, always follow label instructions
  • Never apply undiluted essential oils to skin
  • Never allow your pet to ingest them
  • Avoid the eyes, ears, and mucous membranes
  • Do a small patch test before wider application
  • Never use essential oils on pregnant or nursing animals without veterinary guidance
  • Cats are especially sensitive — many oils safe for dogs are toxic to cats
  • As with the other repellent methods discussed above, the repellent effect fades as the smell fades, so reapplication is necessary

Some oils to avoid entirely around pets — tea tree oil in particular is highly toxic to both dogs and cats, and pennyroyal, wintergreen, and cinnamon oils are also on the do-not-use list. Confirm any product or DIY blend with a veterinarian familiar with essential oil safety before applying to your animal.12

Two Handy Oils Worth a Second Look

There are two other oils worth knowing about, though with a clear-eyed view of their limits. These are:

  • Coconut oil — When applied to the coat, it can help soothe irritated skin and may make it slightly harder for fleas to move through the fur. It is not a stand-alone flea killer, and it can leave floors and furniture greasy, but small amounts rubbed into the coat can be useful during a flare-up. Organic fractionated coconut oil is the form that is best absorbed by pet coats.
  • Neem oil — Diluted in a carrier and sprayed on affected areas, it has traditional use as an insect repellent. Its taste is bitter enough that pets tend to leave it alone once applied. As with any oil, dilute properly and check with your vet, especially if you have a cat in the home.

What Doesn't Work (and What to Skip)

Not every home remedy that circulates online is safe or effective. A few common recommendations to avoid:13

  • Garlic (in any form) — Toxic to both dogs and cats
  • Salt sprinkled in the house — The amount needed to work is toxic if ingested
  • Rubbing alcohol on a pet's skin or on an attached tick — Can worsen a tick bite (can increase likelihood of disease transmission) and irritates skin
  • Undiluted tea tree oil — Fatal even in small amounts
  • Dish soap as a primary flea treatment — Kills adults on contact but does not touch the life cycle
  • Feeding brewer's yeast for flea control — Not shown to work

The general principle: natural does not automatically mean safe, and the fact that something is sold as a home remedy does not mean it has been studied. When in doubt, ask a holistic or integrative veterinarian before using something new.

Work with a Holistic Vet

Integrative and holistic veterinarians take a whole-picture view of flea prevention that goes beyond just killing bugs. They often look at:

  • Diet quality — well-nourished pets with strong skin barriers and strong gut health tend to be less attractive to fleas
  • Immune support through species-appropriate nutrition and targeted supplements
  • Environmental toxin load — reducing exposure to unnecessary chemicals overall
  • Gut health, since a healthy microbiome supports overall resilience
  • Stress and skin health, both of which affect how a pet's body responds to bites

This kind of approach does not produce overnight results the way a strong chemical or prescription product can. But over time, it tends to create an animal whose body is less reactive to occasional flea bites and whose environment does not sustain a large flea population. That is a different definition of "prevention" than most conventional advice offers.

What to Expect

Natural flea control asks more of the pet parent. It is less about applying one product or administering one dose of medication every few weeks and more about weaving several habits into your life — a cleaner yard, a well-vacuumed and steam-cleaned home, weekly bedding washes, dilute rinses during flea season, and a watchful eye.

Natural remedies typically take a little longer to work than heavier products. That does not mean they are not working; it means the approach is building up over time rather than delivering an immediate kill. Consistency is what makes it succeed.

Some pets — particularly those with severe flea allergy dermatitis or ongoing skin infections — may need more targeted and fast-acting care, and that is a conversation to have with your veterinarian. But for most healthy pets, a well-designed natural approach can meaningfully reduce flea burden and keep infestations from taking hold in the first place.

The Bigger Picture

Choosing a more natural approach to fleas is not about being anti-science or anti-modern medicine. It is about being intentional — reducing unnecessary chemical exposure where you reasonably can, supporting the environment your pet lives in, and paying attention to the whole system rather than treating symptoms in isolation.

Your dog or cat is exposed to more environmental chemicals over a lifetime than any previous generation of companion animals. Every choice you make to lighten that load — cleaner food, cleaner water, cleaner air, cleaner flea and tick strategies — adds up over the long stretch of their lives.

Fleas are part of the deal when you live with an animal. They do not have to be a constant source of chemical exposure to control. With some patience, a multi-pronged plan, and the right knowledge, you can keep your pet comfortable and your home flea-free using tools that align with the way you would rather care for them anyway.

Sources and References

  • 2,3,5,7,8,10 AKC Pet Insurance, June 3, 2022
  • 4,6,9,11 The National Canine Cancer Foundation, August 19, 2021
  • 12,13 PetMD, April 18, 2024

item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Both Doberman Pinschers and Boxers are predisposed to heart disease due to a genetic mutation
  • There are genetic tests available for both breeds, but neither veterinarians nor dog parents know much about them
  • The veterinary cardiologist who discovered the gene mutations recommends vets test each Dobie and Boxer in their practice, preferably when they’re still puppies
  • It’s important to stay alert for signs of a potential heart problem in your dog, especially if he or she is a high-risk breed
  • It’s also important to take steps to help your dog avoid heart disease whenever possible

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published January 24, 2018.

Biomarkers are being used more often in veterinary medicine, and based on her work in this field, Dr. Kathryn Meurs, a veterinary cardiologist at the North Carolina State University College of Veterinary Medicine, is encouraging colleagues to make genetic testing part of their regular services.

Some Dobermans and Boxers Are Predisposed to Heart Disease

Biomarkers are molecules that indicate normal or abnormal processes taking place in the body and may be a sign of an underlying condition or disease. These vital nutrients are not found in adequate quantities in most dry foods, and processing further diminishes their bioavailability. Supplying your pet with extra CoQ10 (the reduced form) can insure he has the quantity his body needs to maintain a healthy heart muscle.
  2. Help your dog maintain a lean, fit body with daily exercise appropriate for his age, health and physical condition.
  3. Take excellent care of his dental health. Bacteria from dirty doggy (and human) mouths has been linked to heart valve infections.
  4. Talk to your holistic or integrative veterinarian about cardiovascular support supplements such as ubiquinol, amino acids (taurine, L-arginine and acetyl L-carnitine), hawthorn berries, d-ribose, TMG heart glandulars, and homeopathic and TCM formulas that specifically fit your pet’s symptoms.
  5. Finally, ask your veterinarian for a proBNP blood test, which is a simple blood test that detects early signs of heart disease. If you have a Dobie or a Boxer, also request the Doberman DCM test or the Boxer ARVC test.

  • 2 Veterinary Practice News, November 9, 2017

STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Sardines are small saltwater fish that have been enjoyed by humans for centuries, which your pet can eat as well
  • Research has shown that saltwater fish contains EPA and DHA omega-3 fats that may help boost your pet’s health in several ways
  • Fresh, frozen sardines are available in some parts of the world. When buying canned sardines, look for those packed in water
  • Aside from omega-3 fatty acids, sardines contain some amounts of vitamin B12 and D and selenium, all of which may support your pet
  • The best way to feed sardines to your pet is raw, although the fish can also be dehydrated to help increase shelf life while still retaining all its healthy nutrients

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published September 16, 2022.

As small saltwater fish that thrive in different oceans around the world, sardines are a fixture in the human diet. They’re enjoyed in different ways — from simple recipes to extravagant dishes, these small, fatty fish can offer something for everyone. And that “everyone” can even include your four-legged friend at home.

If you’ve been wondering about feeding sardines to your pet, rest assured they’re one of the healthiest foods to share. They contain DHA and EPA omega-3 fats, which can benefit your pet’s health in several ways. However, there are some things you need to know before feeding your pet these fish.

Did You Know?

While the name “sardines” is accepted throughout the world, it is referred to as “pilchard” in the United Kingdom.1

Omega-3 Is the Star of Sardines

One of the main bioactive compounds of sardines is omega-3 fatty acids, including EPA and DHA. In fact, sardines are considered to be a top source of marine-based omega-3s, along with other fish such as anchovies, salmon, mackerel, trout and herring.2 The benefits of omega-3s on animal health have also been studied for quite some time now. Increasing your pet’s intake of omega-3 fats can positively affect their health in certain areas, such as:

  • Managing osteoarthritis — Increased consumption of omega-3 has been shown to help manage inflammation, especially when it comes to osteoarthritic dogs. One study noted that test dogs who consumed omega-3 had significant improvement in locomotor disability and performance of daily activities.3
  • Boosting skin health — Omega-3 fatty acids may help improve skin in dogs, according to a 1994 study. Researchers gave 16 dogs omega-3 fatty acids that included high levels of EPA. Results showed that the dogs experienced improvement in itchiness, self-trauma, coat character and hair loss compared with administration of ALA (alpha linoleic acid) alone.4
  • Improving cardiac function — Researchers discovered that upping omega-3 intake may help reduce the production of inflammatory cytokines, as well as help reduce muscle loss in dogs diagnosed with dilated cardiomyopathy.5
  • Helping improve growth in newborn puppies — If you’ve been fostering newborn puppies or will be doing so anytime soon, a little bit of omega-3 in their diet may do wonders for them. A 2012 study noted that the fatty acid provided a wide range of health benefits in cognitive, memory, psychomotor, immunologic and retinal function in 48 healthy, newly weaned, 8-week-old Beagle puppies.6

Other Nutrients in Sardines

Aside from omega-3 fatty acids, sardines contain some amounts of vitamin B12 and D and selenium, all of which may support your pet. Vitamin B12, also known as cobalamin, acts as a cofactor for many enzymatic processes in both humans and animals, such as gastrointestinal function, nucleic acid synthesis and amino acid metabolism. In addition, animals can’t synthesize their own vitamin B12, making it a necessary addition to your pet’s diet every now and then.7

Meanwhile, sufficient intake of vitamin D through diet is required by dogs and cats because they cannot produce their own through sun exposure. Vitamin D has been shown to play a role in bone metabolism.8 In the case of selenium, it has been found to play an antioxidant function in dogs, as well as proper thyroid metabolism and reproductive health.9 Sardines provide an excellent source of bioavailable vitamin D.

Fun Fact About Sardines

The name “sardines” references the island of Sardinia in Italy, where this particular fish was once abundant.10

How to Serve Sardines to Your Pet

The best way to feed sardines to your pet is raw, although the fish can also be dehydrated to help increase shelf life while still retaining all its healthy nutrients. Furthermore, sardines, as well as other treats, should only comprise less than 10% of your pet’s daily food intake. Anything more could lead them to overeating, which may introduce potential health problems down the line. The bulk of their nutrition should still come from a whole food, species-appropriate diet.

Now that you know important guidelines on feeding treats to your pet, you can introduce sardines to them with this easy-to-prepare recipe.

Dehydrated Sardine Crisps

Ingredients:

  • 1 can of sardines packed in water

Other equipment needed:

  • Parchment paper
  • Food dehydrator

Procedure:

  1. Drain the sardines.
  2. Place the sardines on top of parchment paper, then place the paper on top of the dehydrator tray.
  3. Dehydrate the sardines at 155 degrees Fahrenheit (68.3 degrees Celsius) for two hours.
  4. Reduce temperature to 140 degrees Fahrenheit (60 degrees Celsius) for four more hours, or until sardines are thoroughly dried.
  5. Store in an airtight container for up to a week.

Note: The sardine crisps can stay fresh in the refrigerator for one week. When stored in the freezer, they can last up to three months.

Top Sardine Producers in the World

The countries that exported the highest amount of sardines are Morocco, Japan, China, Russia and Oman.11

Choose Sustainable, Healthy Sources of Sardines

Fish isn’t ideally recommended as a food or treat for dogs and cats because of the issue of contaminated leftovers from the human food chain (containing high levels of dioxins and PCBs) that end up in pet food.

How does fish become contaminated? According to the Environmental Defense Fund, there are several ways wherein toxins accumulate in fish. The process starts when industrial and agricultural waste end up in oceans. Rainfall can also wash away chemicals into streams and rivers that eventually end up in large bodies of water.12

From there, the chemicals end up in the food that the fish eat, as well as their surroundings. For example, bacteria that come into contact with mercury transforms into methylmercury, which eventually end up in fish. Mercury can also accumulate in fish when it passes through their gills.13 PCBs, which are found in sediments,14 end up in the fatty layers of fish.15

Larger, predatory species of fish tend to have more time to “bioaccumulate” mercury because of their volume and age. Aside from these factors, another contributor to their bioaccumulation of mercury is because of the mercury-infected fish they consume.16

Beware of These Contaminated Fish

Due to the constant dumping of contaminants in the ocean, certain species of fish (especially larger ones) have become highly contaminated. These include shark, swordfish, king mackerel and tilefish.17

Now that you’re aware of how toxins accumulate in fish, here’s what you need to know about feeding them to your pets. Cats shouldn’t consume an excessive amount of seafood because marine-sourced proteins are the richest sources of iodine, a mineral cats need very little of because they are prone to hyperthyroidism (which is exacerbated by dietary iodine).

However, dogs prone to hypothyroidism (a low thyroid) can greatly benefit from whole foods that contain bioavailable iodine, including sardines. Feeding dogs and non-hyperthyroid cats sardines as a treat or meal topper on a regular basis is a great way to provide a rich source of vitamin D, DHA and EPA in whole-food form.

Feeding a base diet of fish protein to dogs or cats isn’t recommended, unless you’re choosing specific nontoxic fish and creating a nutritionally complete homemade diet. More importantly, mercury contamination in large ocean fish is a real and serious problem, not to mention the toxic environment these fish grow in. That being said, sardines are a good choice because of their short lifespan, since they don’t live long enough to accumulate notable levels of toxins.

For a few years after the Fukushima nuclear accident in Japan, all of the fish (including sardines) harvested from that bay area had unhealthy levels of radiation contamination, but thankfully those regional sardines have since tested below detectable levels, and there are a multitude of different types of sardines found throughout the world you can choose from that are cleaner.

The Blue Zone of Sardinia

The island of Sardinia is designated as a “blue zone.” This means that there’s a high concentration of centenarians living there, which is attributed to several factors, including the healthy diet they eat and their low-stress environment. Sardinian elders generally get more exercise as well.18

When it comes to choosing sardines, Steve Brown, a renowned expert on fresh food diets for pets, only recommends feeding fresh sardines (found locally or in the freezer section of some groceries in some parts of the world) or canned sardines packed in water or olive oil (pending no issues digesting healthy fats). Be sure to read the label carefully, as the sardines may be packed in other oils, such as soy.19

Remember Not to Solely Rely on Sardines for Proper Nutrition

While sardines contain an assortment of nutrients, most notably omega-3 fats, you shouldn’t rely on this fish solely for proper nutrition. Feed your pet a species-appropriate, nutritionally complete diet using raw or lightly cooked ingredients. Use sardines (one piece per 20 pounds of body weight) as a tasty yet nutritious treat or food topper that your pet will look forward to eating every now and then.

Sources and References

  • 1 Britannica, “Sardine”
  • 2 BioMed Research International, August 5, 2022, Abstract
  • 3 J Lab Clin Med, March 2000; 135(3): 275-286
  • 4 Veterinary Dermatology, September 1994; 5(3): 99-104
  • 5 J Vet Intern Med, 1998 November-December; 12(6): 440-448
  • 6 J Am Vet Med Assoc, September 1, 2012; 241(5): 583-594
  • 7 MSPCA, “Cobalamin Deficiency”
  • 8 Metabolites. 2020 December 3; 10(12): 496, Abstract
  • 9 Animals (Basel). 2021 February 6; 11(2): 418, Abstract
  • 10 New World Encyclopedia, “Sardine”
  • 11 OEC, “Sardines, brisling, sprats, frozen, whole”
  • 12,13,15 EDF Seafood Selector, “Common questions about contaminants in seafood” (Archived)
  • 14 National Ocean Service, “What Are PCBs?”
  • 16 FoodPrint, “So Where Does All That Mercury in Fish Come From?”
  • 17 Environ Health Perspect. 2012 February 22; 120(6): 790-798, Results
  • 18 NBC News, June 10, 2019
  • 19 YouTube, Rodney Habib, July 24, 2016

The island of Sardinia is designated as a “blue zone.” This means that there’s a high concentration of centenarians living there, which is attributed to several factors, including the healthy diet they eat and their low-stress environment. Sardinian elders generally get more exercise as well.18

When it comes to choosing sardines, Steve Brown, a renowned expert on fresh food diets for pets, only recommends feeding fresh sardines (found locally or in the freezer section of some groceries in some parts of the world) or canned sardines packed in water or olive oil (pending no issues digesting healthy fats). Be sure to read the label carefully, as the sardines may be packed in other oils, such as soy.19

Remember Not to Solely Rely on Sardines for Proper Nutrition

While sardines contain an assortment of nutrients, most notably omega-3 fats, you shouldn’t rely on this fish solely for proper nutrition. Feed your pet a species-appropriate, nutritionally complete diet using raw or lightly cooked ingredients. Use sardines (one piece per 20 pounds of body weight) as a tasty yet nutritious treat or food topper that your pet will look forward to eating every now and then.
